purpose: Record what each shell does with the constructs that are not in POSIX, so a script's choice of interpreter is a measured fact rather than a habit.
note: Columns are shell implementations, not paths, because `/bin/sh` is not one program: it is bash on macOS and dash on Debian and Ubuntu. `cargo xtask posix-divergence` re-measures each implementation and then decides which column `/bin/sh` on the runner belongs to by running the same scripts through it — so the answer to `what is /bin/sh here` comes from behaviour rather than from a version string. Most of these diverge in silence: only substring-expansion reports an error. A construct whose columns disagree is a reason a script names its interpreter, and a reason de-shell will not lower it without one.

cases.name: ansi-c-quoting-in-a-case-pattern
cases.script:
case "a
b" in *$'\n'*) echo MATCHED ;; *) echo NO_MATCH ;; esac
cases.note: A newline check written with $'\n' silently passes everything under a shell without ANSI-C quoting: the pattern becomes the literal characters and never matches.

cases.name: ansi-c-quoting-expansion
cases.note: Without ANSI-C quoting the word is left as written, so a tab becomes four characters.

cases.name: double-bracket-test
cases.note: `[[` is a keyword, not a builtin. A shell without it runs `[[` as a command, which fails, so a guard written this way inverts in silence.

cases.name: brace-expansion
cases.note: Without brace expansion the word is one literal argument rather than two.

cases.name: substring-expansion
cases.note: The one on this list that fails loudly: a shell without it reports a syntax error instead of running.

cases.name: local-in-a-function
cases.note: Not in POSIX, and every shell measured here has it anyway.

cases.name: echo-suppress-newline
cases.note: Whether `-n` is an option or a word to print.

cases.name: echo-backslash-in-a-variable
cases.note: Whether the echo builtin rescans its arguments for escapes.
